name: Perceived Naturalness of Edinburgh Street View (1–7 rating)
description:
Rebuilt from Hyam (2017), "Automated Image Sampling and Classification Can Be Used to Explore Perceived Naturalness of Urban Spaces", PLOS ONE 12(1): e0169357.

The paper sampled Google Street View views on a regular grid across Edinburgh, scored each automatically with Google Vision labels (Calculated Semantic Naturalness), and then had a human panel rate 100 of them, 20 from each quintile of the automatic score, for perceived naturalness. Images appear one at a time in a different random order for each participant, with seven buttons from 1 (not natural) to 7 (natural); clicking a button scores the image and moves on, exactly as in the paper. Records are keyed by the paper's image id (e.g. sv315), so new ratings can be joined to the paper's open data (automatic naturalness, panel means, deprivation index) in S1/S2. The paper found the automatic score correlated with human perceived naturalness, the idea behind many later street-view greenery and naturalness models.

Images: Google Street View (© Google), re-fetched with the panorama ids and headings the author published in S2/S3 (Google does not allow redistributing the original files). 44 views come from the very same 2012–2015 panoramas; for the 55 whose panorama is no longer served, the nearest current panorama at the same spot is used, turned to face the same sample point.

Differences from the original study: (1) 99 instead of 100 images: one view is now privacy-blurred by Google and is left out; (2) 55 views are newer panoramas from the same locations (see above), so seasons and details can differ from what the panel saw; (3) the panel was 15 staff and associates of the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh; this template is open to any sample and asks gender and age only.
